entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: DONALD DICKEY

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Interview conducted by Bob Zybach and Neil Vanderburg at the Green Valley Care Center, August 18, 1990, with Donald and Maxine Dickey.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. FAMILY HISTORY

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Donald, would you mind just saying hello or something, to just see if this recorder is working? Then I'll check it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Hi, I'm glad to be part of this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Don, can you tell me what year you were born and where you were born.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Born, October 20, 1914 at Yamhill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your father's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: James A. Dickey.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was he doing in Yamhill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was a farmer down there. We had 50 acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he born in Yamhill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he was born up by Buell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Buell, Oregon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's over by Willamina, Sheridan, in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you remember his parents?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, his parents were dead, they died when he was 15 or 16.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they farming in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had . . I think they had 320 acres. They raised livestock mainly. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they both died at about the same time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, when they was 58, 59 something like that. Within a year or two anyway of each other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So were the deaths related, was it an epidemic, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think one of them had cancer, but I'm not sure, and I don't know about the other one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then your father, did he continue working on the family farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was three boys and three or four girls, so they divided the family farm up, and my dad had a 40 acre piece of it he and one of his sisters lived on. And I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: don't know for how long, till his sister got married I guess. Then dad married my mother in 1903 and they lived there on the 40 acres for a while then they sold it and moved down to Yamhill. And I don't know whether they rented the 10 acres that they were on for a while or not, I think maybe they did, but then they bought 50 acres out southwest of Yamhill 4-1/2 miles, a little area they called . . . anyway, it was clay, some kind of a gulch out there. And they got a pretty good farm out there. They had to build a house and barn, that stuff. And we had dairy cows. And the soil was kind of hard to work, but if you worked it good and kept at it you raised good crops on it. And in 1928 we moved from Yamhill up to Berry Creek, and one of the reasons for it was they wanted to get closer to Oregon State [University]. My older brother was going to Oregon State, and my youngest brother was a couple of years younger than I was. We were still in grade school when we moved up there. Then we went to Airlie to high school, and I went to Oregon State and I graduated high school in '37, or '33, and didn't get started at Oregon State till '37, on account of there weren't any money trees growing in the back yard in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the reason your folks moved to Berry Creek was to get the family closer to Oregon State?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was your father a college graduate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but he was pretty well educated. So was my mother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, going back to your mother's family, do you know where she was born?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was born back in Eddyville, Nebraska.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eddyville Nebraska?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Um hmm. And they moved out in 1893 to Salem. They had a cousin or something over there. They lived there a year or two and then they moved over by Sheridan on Mill Creek, and they, I don't know, they were there for several years I guess, then about 1900 or 1901 or 2 her folks moved over in Tillamook County near Hemlock. And she and Dad got married in 1903 and came back to live on the 40 acres that was part of his dad's old homestead. Then they moved to Yamhill and eventually Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your mother's family's maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Blanchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Blanchard? Do you know her mother's maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bolton.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember either of her parents?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother's parents?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My grandmother, she was one of the nicest little old ladies that I ever knew. Never said anything bad about anybody. And she lived till she was 66, I think. 1933 or sometime about then. And all of us boys were born down at Yamhill, my brothers, just 3 of us, and then we moved up to Berry Creek, and there, why, my older brother worked in California and different places, and I graduated from Oregon State and went to work for the [Oregon] Game Commission for a while. And World War II was on. So chasing pheasants didn't seem too necessary, since there were a lot of pheasants in the valley anyway. So I took a job with the US Fish and Wildlife Service killing the ground squirrels around Camp White where they'd found them carrying the plague the year before. From there they transferred me to Vanport. I was there at Vanport, let's see, went to Camp White, then they transferred me to Vanport in August and they transferred me to Eugene in February. And I was working on extermination projects, and supposedly I killed 50,000 rats the first 5 months that I was in Eugene. So I, after about 4 years, they decided to pull their money out of the project, they were going to put me someplace else, but I didn't like the payoff, so I stayed and took over the job at Eugene. And worked there, Eugene, Cottage Grove, Junction City, Oakridge, Coburg, and I stayed pretty busy. I worked for a while in Florence, till I got the rats pretty well cleaned up down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Florence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Florence.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I worked 35 years on rodent control. Not completely on rodent control, because I developed a line of rodent bait called Ortho Rodent Bait. And retired in 1980 and sold the bait business to a young fellow by the name of Doug Freeman. And he's operating it out of Coburg now.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Harrisburg.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Harrisburg. Where else do you want me to go from there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll just keep going back and then bringing it forward and then we'll concentrate on Berry Creek in a bit. When you graduated from Oregon State, what was your degree in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fish and Game Management.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were able to capitalize on that pretty much. How about your older brother?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was taking mining engineering, and they closed the mining school before he got out. And besides, he started in '26 and by '29 things was getting a little rough. Anyway, he got a job in a mine down in California, and instead of finishing up why he worked down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your younger brother, did he go to Oregon State?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he. . . well, my father died in 1942. He died on my birthday, and was buried on my younger brother's birthday. And then my younger brother, we were married by that time, Maxine and I, so my younger brother stayed around the farm for a long time. And my mother remarried after a while, and then my brother got so that he had trouble with his lungs or something because of the cold wind that blew down they lived over by, what's the name of that place where they lived, Maxine? Where was it they lived over there? Wren. And the wind blew down through that gap there from Kings Valley in the wintertime, and my brother was working hard and he had trouble with his lungs or something, so he decided he had better get out of there so he moved to Arizona, and well, they had given him in 1952 ten years to live because he'd had

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Holocystic kidneys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Holocystic kidneys. He lived 30 years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's go back real briefly to 1893 when your grandparents came with your mother out to Oregon. Did they come by train?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they came by train.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From Nebraska.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From Nebraska.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know why they came to Oregon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he had a store, her dad had a store with some other fellow, and I'm not sure that they were getting along too well. They had some relatives out here at Salem. And Oregon was kind of a popular place to come, so they came out here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They just heard it was a nice place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your father's folks? Do you know why they came to Oregon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father's family? Well they came in 1853. From Lone Jack, Missouri, and I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: think it was just part of the western migration, probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just free land? Do you know if there were any stories in your family about coming across on the [Oregon] trail?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: No, we haven't.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not, really.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so do you know how your father and mother met?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they lived in the same area down there by Buell. And I might tell you a little interesting side story on that. My dad and mother got married and they'd go out on a Sunday for a buggy ride. And of course she come in later than dad, why she didn't know who was related to who, she'd heard these stories about various people. So one Sunday they were out and met somebody on the road and exchanged greetings with them and drove on, and my mother said, "Did you hear that story about . . " I don't know what the story was about. And dad says, "Oh, you can't tell stories about her, she's my cousin." Mother said she was beginning to think he was related to everybody in the area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is any of that land still in the family? The donation land claim?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. It wasn't what I'd call real hot farm land. It was more cattle than anything, so . . . Incidently, we have been back to Lone Jack, where my great grandfather homesteaded.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I think that was 1835, wasn't it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that country looks a good deal like where they settled out here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he picked land out here in Oregon that was real similar to what they left in Missouri?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: We have become good friends with those people, and they have been out to visit us, and he sent me a picture to hang on my wall, you know, because he knows I do genealogy, and with a picture of the old homestead, he's got an "X" on it where the old well was, which is still there, and where the barn was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In Lone Jack?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yes. And they have sent us a lot of horseshoes. Because he has a metal detector he picks out all the horseshoes. And made all of our kids clocks out of the wood from this old barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the Dickey homestead in Lone Jack.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's interesting, the old barn was made out of walnut and oak. And he saved some pieces. I think the four clocks we have are made from oak. Imagine making a barn from oak and walnut? You asked about stories on the trail. I only remember one that they told, they come up just looking over a ridge and here was a bunch of stuff waving on ahead, and they were ready to group up and then discovered it was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: willows instead of a bunch of Indians.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know where that occurred, about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that's the one story that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the one story that I remember him telling. That was my dad's story.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any stories about when they first set up the donation land claim, or the homestead?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I asked my dad how come they settled back there, and he said, "well, I think

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: they wanted wood and water." There was still good land out here in the valley, I'm sure, in 1853. But then the other part of the family had come earlier, and they had settled over there, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there were two groups of Dickeys, that .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was Dickey, and Bolyjacks, my grandfather married a Bolyjack girl. And Newbergs, one of the Newbergs married another Bolyjack girl, and Lackeys has married another Bolyjack girl. There were three Bolyjack girls. They were all in the same general area down there. And then there was some brothers of my dad that settled down there too.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. SNOW STORMS

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know if have any family stories come through about, say, the flood of 1861 or the snow storm in 1883? Do you know anything about those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Snowstorm, yes. The flood I don't. I don't know much about the snowstorm. But it snowed and snowed and snowed. Dad used to talk about that. He talked about finally it quit snowing and they decided they wanted to hike over to some friends or family, or something for a visit and he said that that old snow was piled up and kind of slippery on the surface. And dad was walking with a stick with a nail in the end of it. He got down on the side of a hill and he started slipping and sliding down, he said his mother was standing out there "Jim, Jim, Jim, Jim, Jim!" He didn't get hurt or anything, just down untill he stopped.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Wasn't that your grandfather that was sliding down the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah, his grandfather. His name was Jim, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your dad was Jim, Jr.?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: He was James Abraham.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was Jim anyway. I never heard him called Jim, Jr.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Okay. Then that was the snowstorm in 1883?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm sure that's when it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Donald, he had only one eye. Do you know how he lost his eye? Your grandfather?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he fell in a fire, but I'm not sure about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your grandfather was the person that this story is about. Did he, had he lost that eye by the time he was a child, or could that have been the snowstorm of 1861 maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because my dad wasn't born untill 1872.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and your dad could remember the story.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well my dad was along when his dad was sliding down the hill and his mother was saying "Jim, Jim, Jim, Jim, Jim."

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: His dad was the last of the Dickeys, I mean the youngest child.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, on your father, when you had a snowstorm in, was it 1937, on Berry Creek, did he compare that to that earlier one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we couldn't get out to the road for two days, we lived back about 3/8's of a mile off the main road. We didn't get any mail for three days. We had 3 feet of snow. With what, they had Sunday school over at the school house at Berry Creek there, so we went over and we got back and ate lunch, and my dad looked out and it was still snowing 6-7 inches. We had an old barn there on Berry Creek, and dad didn't think it was too stable, and so he says I think we'd better start shoveling snow off the barn. So we shoveled snow off the barn till 5:00, then we had to start doing chores and take cows in, the horses, feed the chickens and stuff. I had about 8 or 10 or 12 sheep out behind the fence that stayed under a big fir tree where I'd been feeding them. And at 5:00 they'd been out there. At 6:00 when I got around to get out feeding them, I took out a load of hay and some grain and they were gone back up the hill into other timber. By that time there was a foot of snow. And I thought boy if I don't get them down off that hill tonight I'll never get them. So I went out and chased them down off the hill and got them feeding under the tree, and figured they'd stay there. So when I went into the house I measured the snow and there was, I think there was 16 inches on the ground at 7:00. At 9:00 there was 30 inches of snow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. Can you recall any snows since that time that were that bad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well we had one down here a few years back, that was almost that bad. In 1969 down here it was that bad. Out west of Eugene here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: It was '69.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: '69, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was almost as bad as the '37 snow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was worse out here in some places. They told me out, oh just this side of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the mountains, out there they had four feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did your dad say about the one in 1937? Could he remember any that were any worse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he wasn't particularly worried about it. They had one in [the winter of] 1919- 1920 that snowed every day for 30 days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the one in 1919 was even worse.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it never did pile up 3 feet of snow, but it must have been 25 inches or so. I don't know whether you'll put this in or not. But people didn't have inside facilities then, so every day we had to shovel the snow to get to the little house out back and it got piled up so along the path that I couldn't see over it. I would have only been about 5 years old at the time. I used to go out and help shovel the snow. We've had that kind, and we know we'll have it again.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. BERRY CREEK NEIGHBORS

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you moved to Berry Creek then was 1928?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: April 1928.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the reason was just to get closer to the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's the main reason. We also had traded 50 acres for 160 acres. We had more land, had some timber on it and stuff. We cut posts and timber and stuff and wood to sell, and then we would add logs for Coote and Cornutt. Several years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, your family traded 50 acres. Was that part of the donation land claim?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no this was the new deal that they bought after they left Buell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The family that stayed back in the donation land claim, were they sorry to see your dad leave or do you remember any stories about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think they'd all left. Or about all left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh I see. Okay. And then, your family moved to Berry Creek. Was there a home there at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. We lived there until the [U.S.] Army took over in '42.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you build the house there or was there already a house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was a house already there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the families that lived in Berry Creek in 1928?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh, when we moved up there where Neil [Vanderburg] lived and his folks, people by the name of Perkins lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Perkins?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Um hmm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Perkins was one of these guys that didn't always watch his language to close. So over the hill from Perkins . . . Perkins had 120 acres, that's right isn't it Neil?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And was Walter Brinkley. He was a bachelor, or he was widower I guess. His wife had died. So Walter had me trap the gophers for him, out in the hay field, and he had some pretty big gophers, quite a lot of them. One Sunday morning I rode down to check my traps, came back and I had a pretty big one I brought back up to show him. And old Perkins, he looked at him, said "Boy he's ugly. That ugly son-of-a- bitch is uglier than I am!" Then after Perkins left there, people by the name of Keller lived there, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Keller?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Did you buy it from Keller?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Rapher lived there when we moved there. He was renting the place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well I guess he came after Keller.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. That's the first one I knew.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, on Brinkley, that hill by Brinkley's place, did you call that Brinkley's Hill, do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just a hill there that we went over to go to town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything in particular about Brinkley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was a real nice fellow. He had a lost son, and he had a daughter that lived with his brother-in-law, I think. He'd lost his wife. He farmed there for three or four years, then he moved up by Corvallis. On the Wiles place, I think. Or part of it. And married a nice lady. Maxine and I used to stop in and see them now and then. He was a real nice gentleman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who moved into Brinkley's place after he left?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that a livestock dealer over in Monmouth rented it from him. And I don't know whether they sold it or what happened after that. It was a good place for livestock there, and sheep and stuff on it. Good place to hunt pheasants, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember, were there always pheasants there when . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was when we moved there untill '42 when we moved away, there were still pheasants there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how long Brinkley had lived there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I suspect three or four or five years before we were there, I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there were just a, in the 1920's a fair number of families had moved in about that time?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: When did the Hauges, your parents' good friend Carl Hauge, when did they move in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Carl Hauge is another, he rented about 500 acres just west of our place, and actually the place belonged to a brother or cousin; I think it belonged to a cousin. Carl and his wife raised sheep, they were real nice people. And somehow or another Carl got the idea that they were going to do something to the place besides rent it, so he and his wife moved up to Sauvies Island with their sheep. Then they moved back down to Beaver Creek, this side [south] of Corvallis, with their sheep. I don't know whether his wife had

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: we find ow about these people will be all we know about them. So we were on the

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hauges and they had just moved from Sauvie's Island down to Beaver Creek. And I think you said his wife had died of cancer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She died while there and Carl sold his sheep and moved to Alaska for fishing and various things up there. He was as old as my dad was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did his family move to the Berry Creek area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Carl Hauge?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know for sure, but Carl and his wife Lucy were from Switzerland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were Swiss?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Um hmm. And he could talk six or seven different languages. He was a real sharp guy, a real nice guy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he raised sheep mostly?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's what he did when we were there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you say that was to the west of your place. Would that have been.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the first place west of our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was before the Hanish's lived there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Hanish lived on 40 acres to the left. This place that Carl Hauge lived on is the place that Cooper Brothers built the sawmill on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Cooper Brothers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Um hmm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Hauges, do you know about what year he moved in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know what year Hauge moved in there, but he moved out in 1930 I think it was.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: And is that when Cooper Brothers built the mill? Did they build the mill in 1930?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They built the mill in 1929 or '30, I don't remember which. Both Coote and Cornutt and the Cooper Brothers built their mill about the same time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, to back up a little bit, the sheep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can I interject? Cooper's Mill is now Mountain Fir Mill in Independence. They moved to Independence.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well they split up, too. Hap took half, and Frank [Cooper].

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Frank Cooper married a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Frank Cooper married a school teacher that his older brother Hap didn't like. So they sort of split the thing in half.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim Hanish said that going to the west of his place, back in the hills there, that he found sheep skulls with curved horns, that it must have been an earlier.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He found what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sheep skulls with curved horns to them. Do you know anything about the sheep that were raised in that area, was there anything unusual about those sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were just ordinary sheep. I think Jim Hanish has got delusions. [Jim Hanish showed me one of those skulls. I didn't think it was worth upsetting Donald though. NV]
bracketed_corrections: [Jim Hanish showed me one of those skulls. I didn't think it was worth upsetting Donald though. NV]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. He remembered them wrong. He said that Brinkley told him of two or three Indian sites, including one on top of Forest Peak. Do you recall hearing anything about any Indian sites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only Indian stuff I knew about was down on our place, in a little alfalfa field next to the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what types of things can you recall from that Indian site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we found arrowheads and occasionally part of a deal that you hammered out

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: grain in or whatever, and maybe part of a vessel, but nothing real good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you keep any of those things?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, probably some arrowheads, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't have them anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think my kid brother [Ken] collected them. No, I never bothered much collecting arrowheads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Donald, didn't you have irrigation rights on that creek was one of the reasons you moved there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we acquired irrigation rights on it about 1932 or '33, and irrigated about 3 acres of alfalfa, and a little bit of other stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had a real good garden.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It helped.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You moved there in '28. That was right before the stock market crash. Did the neighborhood, or did the method of making a living in that neighborhood change very much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were farmers and that's all they did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it didn't have too much of an impact on the local people.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The other people that lived there back on this place that Hanish lived on and this fellow Bass who bought the place from, his brother lived there for a while, six months or so, and I guess Hanish was the next guy that guy that lived there. Then, there was, well when I started to school there was people that lived around on the hill, the Folks hill, around on the east side of it, the kids came to school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the Folks family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wasn't the Folks family, I don't remember their name. They rented, or maybe they worked for Folks. Then, up on top of the hill there, going toward Tampico, there were a couple of houses that renters lived in now and then that worked in the sawmill. One fellow's name was Gardner and the other fellows name was Vain as I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Vain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Vain, V-A-I-N.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then there was a house, part of the hill on over towards Tampico, there was a lady that lived there, and I can't remember what her name was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was up on the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was down on the other side right on the point of the hill. And she raised some livestock and stuff on it. Then beyond that why it was mostly farmland. Joe Brown, or whatever his name was over on Forest Peak and around on that side of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a man named Mallow, Reese Mallow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He lived on Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think he owned some land on the Berry Creek side there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so. He might have, but I don't remember it. I remember the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: My dad bought a load of hay from him, but I don't know where he lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the site where the Indian site was, did you ever see any evidence of any old trails or old wagon roads through your property?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was the place we crossed the creek down there, but it was no old trail or anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the creek crossing, could a wagon have crossed there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was that located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do you know where our place was?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About the middle of the place at the south end.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About the middle of your place on the south end of your place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then that was the crossing of Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't think they used it for a crossing for getting anywhere, just used for the farm, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How about on Savage Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't think there was any major crossing on that. There was a bridge lower down just above . . . Savage Creek came just about to the corner of, southeast corner of our place. As a matter of fact a little of it cut through our place. And there was a bridge across Savage Creek just above where it came through our place. Mostly it was on [Joe] Smith's property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where the road is now, was that road in at Tampico at that time? Was there a road up over the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean the Tampico Road, was it in at that time?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they improved it a lot about 1930 [1938: NV] or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Prior to that time could you take wagons over it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, you could take cars over it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: in the summertime.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I suspect in the winter too. Summer would have been a better bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What can you remember about Joe Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Joe Smith? Joe was a hard worker, and so was his son John. And Joe had a hankering to win himself a little bit of money playing poker. So one story I remember about Joe, he won enough to buy a Hudson car one night in Corvallis. There was several of those guys around in Corvallis that got together and played poker once a week or whatever. I remember one other story about Joe, I worked in the harvest field for him two or three summers. We came in one day and it had been particularly dusty. We'd worked hard from 7:00 to noon, come in to. . . Mrs. Smith always cooked dinner for us. She was a good cook, too. So we'd washed up, Joe was the last one to wash up. He came in with a white towel and he looked at his wife, I forget her first name, and he says "See you got my picture on here [the towel]." You should have seen her. His face really was dirty!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about Greenberry Smith? Or did they ever talk about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Greenberry Smith was south of Corvallis, and I don't really know, there were stories but I don't remember any of them particularly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about any Indians in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There weren't any Indians when we got there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And there's no stories about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never heard any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about black people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Black people?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No black people either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about the Chinese in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No Chinese.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So by the time you were there, there were no stories about any other groups and there was mostly sustenance farmers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was just a farm community and I don't think there was any Chinese or any black people, or any Indians around. Well, the exception old Bud Bass might have been part Indian, but I would not say yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when your family moved there, had they started doing any mill work by that time, was anybody logging in that neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They started in the next year building sawmills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there weren't any sawmills at the first?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The first was 1929 or '30 I think. Then along about '35 Bennett Brothers built a sawmill up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the first mill that caine in, who built that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think Cooper Brothers built the first one, and Coote and Cornutt right away afterwards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the Cooper Brothers, did they live in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived out at Airlie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where did they build their mill at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up on Carl Hauge's place, just west of our place, about 3/4 of a mile up in the woods west of where Carl Hauge lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. What kind of mill was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a little second growth mill. They sawed ties and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. WILDLIFE

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any old growth timber in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The old growth timber was too big for those little mills. There wasn't enough old growth timber to shake your fist at anyway. The only stuff that might have been called old growth was this patch that I mentioned that belonged to Silver Falls

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Logging Co. And some of it might have been considered old growth, although my dad referred to it as bastard growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bastard growth. Do you remember any difference between yellow fir and red fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up there, I don't, I heard of yellow fir and red fir both, but it was all just Doug fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anybody call the larger trees "grandfather trees?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Say it again?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall them being called "grandfather trees," the larger trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandfather trees? No, there wasn't, oh, maybe 40 or 50 of those big old growth trees out by the creek anyway. A fellow from Silverton cut them for 16" wood for Sam Yates from Salem. That's all the old growth. I do recall though that there were three kinds of owls there. There was a screech owl, and an old hoot owl or a horned owl. Then there was the one in between. I always thought the one in between was another screech owl, and I looked him up recently. It undoubtedly was a spotted owl. And it lived out in the second growth timber, oak, and maple, and second growth fir. And I never did see one in the old growth fir. Seen a coon or two parked up the old growth fir. No spotted owls. So I have a big question or two about spotted owls in my mind.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Seeing as how your background is in Fish and Wildlife, and you've identified this owl, in second growth in that area, can you recall how common they were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The owls?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we'd see them every few nights in the summertime. Not so often in the wintertime.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I wanted to ask you some questions about the fish and wildlife in the area, this might be a good time and then we can go back to the families. Can you recall beaver in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No beaver on Berry Creek, there might have been on Soap Creek, but I don't know. No beaver on Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bears? I mentioned a prune orchard back in one of those homesteads? We went back there deer hunting one fall and an old bear had been back there feasting on prunes. But I never did see one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the bears weren't real common?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No they weren't real common.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the prune orchard, do you know when that was planted or who planted it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't, if I could remember the name of the homestead it might be right, but my guess was the trees were 10-15 years old when we moved up there. That's purely a guess, but I think it'd be pretty close.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any stories about Mennonites in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Kilmers were Mennonites.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh the Kilmers were? Okay, can you tell me anything about the Kilmer family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Kilmers, one bunch of them lived back there where Hanish bought that 40 acres, another bunch lived out there at the old Joe Smith place, then there was a house or two across the road on the south side of Berry Creek, which probably belonged to Kilmers. But I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there Kilmers still living there when your family moved there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were gone. Well, with one exception. One of the Kilmers worked for Joe Smith, and he lived out there on Joe's place in a little tenant house, a real nice

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: fellow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did the Kilmers move?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were saying that the graveyard next to your house was a Kilmer graveyard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't next to our house, it was out on the Smith place next to the road. And I don't know, I suppose there was what half a dozen or a dozen graves, Neil?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, probably nine or ten.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never did count them. But part of those were Kilmers I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a couple of babies buried there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember specifics because I wasn't particularly interested in cemeteries then. I have to be now because my wife does genealogy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But at that time was that the only cemetery in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the school that your wife taught at. Was that called the Berry Creek School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear it called the Savage Creek School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that would have been earlier. I don't think. . . they called it Berry Creek after we were up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We were kind of going over the Kilmer's prune orchard. But we were going over some of the fish and wildlife. Can you remember geese and ducks through that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't Kilmer's prune orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh okay, let's back up to that then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No there wasn't. . . you know, occasionally a goose or duck flew over, geese flew over in the spring and the fall, oh some of the other birds migrated south and north in the fall and spring. I remember the first time I ever saw a buzzard migration, along about the first of October. I looked up in the sky to the north. Here come a buzzard. Here come another buzzard. Here come another buzzard, and I'll bet those buzzards flew over there for two hours, one at a time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Other than the migrating birds, you said there were pheasant in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was pheasants. Most of the pheasants were down further east, down on Joe Smith's place and Neil's place and down in there. There were pheasants and valley quail and bob white quail. And then also up in our part there was ruffed grouse, and there was some ruffed grouse down in Joe Smith's place down in the swamp down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Joe Smith had kind of a lake next to his place didn't he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not when we were there. I notice there's one there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was a swamp?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have a name to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just a swamp. It was a good place to run jackrabbits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The field, you had gophers, jackrabbits, four or five types of birds. Did that snow in 1937 affect any of those animal populations?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It didn't seem to have had an impact? How about the deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well the deer were up in the woods. There weren't too many deer then, like there were later. I don't think the deer had any trouble, I mean there was plenty of feed up there and not that many deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any elk in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I don't think there were any elk. There were coyotes and bobcats occasionally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about a cougar? Did you ever recall a cougar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well this fellow from Salem that was cutting the wood from old growth into 16" or four-foot cord wood for Sam Yates was up there in the snow one winter, and he found a cat track that was about so big, that he figured was a cougar, and I think that he found it and he had trailed it one night when he had been down to our place. In fact, he was a little nervous about it. But that's the only time I remember cougar. There were bobcats in there, they killed some of our neighbor's sheep. Cougar probably, I mean likely. Bear occasionally through there. Mainly those were pretty scarce. They had hounds in there. A fellow by the name of Wilson lived over by Airlie had sheep and he had hounds and he ran bear and cougar and that sort of stuff, to protect his sheep. Not so much over there, but he ran sheep over, east of Kings Valley, and I think he ran bear over there with his dogs to protect the sheep.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. FARMING AND MILLING

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did your family have sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we had a dozen or so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What other kinds of animals did you raise?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had goats for a while to get rid of poison oak and brush. Otherwise we had 10 or 12 head of cattle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A team. Two horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Orchards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Orchards? We had four acres of prunes and about an acre of apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you plant the prunes yourselves?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No they were there when we got there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who put those orchards in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember who you bought your place from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do I remember who we bought the place from? Bass. But he was too lazy to put in an orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was somebody before him maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It had to be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did. . . Okay, the Coopers put a mill in about 1930.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, '29 or '30.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what time did Coote move into the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About the same time. I may be off a year, but I think they both had them in about 1930.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then, when Coote put his first mill in, with a pond?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he had a little pond in Savage Creek, and then his second mill he built up on the side of the hill around to the left. And he didn't have a pond there. Or I don't think he did, did he Neil?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that the one he had the flume on? That he brought the logs down the side of the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. I worked up there one summer. I don't remember any flume.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well there was a flume came down into Savage Creek there up around the corner from the mill that was still there when I got there. 1935.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't remember that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They used to pull logs up with teams of horses and then roll it onto the flume and slide it down into the. . . I thought there was a pond in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was a pond down at Coote's first mill. He might have had a flume I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think that's where it was, that first mill. I climbed up that flume. Steep.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember my dad logging down that steep hill there. He'd get started down the hill and he'd throw the line and holler "Giyyap!" Those teams Got, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that your dad's horses, that he logged with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well he farmed with them and logged with them. The best team I ever saw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember their names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cap and Bill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cap and Bill, huh. What kind of horses were they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, work horses I guess. I don't remember what, which was which. Bill, old Bill was a bay horse, white feet, and Cap was a brown horse. Dad said they were a willing team. Cap was willing to do all the work, and Bill was willing to let him. But they'd. . . I remember one day we was trying to clear a log out of Berry Creek down there so that it wouldn't block things up and got it twisted around, and it wasn't coming out, and they both got mad, and boy that lo flew out of there. It wasn't a very big log either. When they decided to move something it moved.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Is that the same team you had when I was there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Okay. I got a picture of that. While I was putting hay or something in the barn or something after his father'd had his stroke just about the time we got married.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We were driving the team with a hay fork.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the same team you drove on the bundle wagon isn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I remember that team.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you when you first moved to Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How old were the horses?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you do for fun in your time off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't have much time off. Hoed the garden, fished occasionally, hunted a little. Mostly you worked.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you do any reading or play cards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, we played cards in the wintertime. We played pinochle and I don't know two or three other games, my brothers and my dad and I and . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: You were always visiting with the Hauges.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we visited with the Hauges quite a bit. He was always, they always had some interesting stories to tell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Hauges? Can you recall any of those stories?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: We must still have those letters he used to write us from up in Alaska.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I remember one of them, they's telling about this one family member that had a big dinner, well she ate and ate and ate. I don't remember the rest of the story. You'd sit there and laugh till you thought you was gonna bust

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. . . I was gone by that time, going to college.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've been trying to figure out where they lived. There was a dairy down there north of you. You turned in just before the Y at Airlie and then came back towards Airlie. Do you know who had that? We hauled some hay in there one time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Are you talking about the place beyond the Brinkley place?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think probably so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goodwin's owned the property and I can't remember who else owned that now. Then there was, oh, what was Kenneth Dodson's granddad's name?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Dodson, I suppose

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wasn't Dodson. Anyway, he was a little short old guy about 80 years old.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Abercrombie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Abercrombies lived back there . . . Cox, Cox, old man Cox they called him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cox? Where did he live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He lived north of our place. His place would have been in Polk County. At least most of it. And he was quite an old character. And then there was a place that belonged to Green that was up north and west from Hauge's place. And I think part of that may have been in Benton County.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the. Hauges lived to the northwest, lets see, to the north and west of your property. That would have been off Staats Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So the west ones were up kind of towards the hills up in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there quite a few families that lived in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just Greens and Hauges is all I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Greens and Hauges? How about the Chaffens?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Chaffens? They lived up on the Savage [at the head of it. NV], or close to Savage Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did those families do for a living?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Greens raised livestock. And Carl Hauge raised livestock. And I don't know what Chaffen did for a living. I guess he milked a few cows and took out some cream or something to sell occasionally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But there was no logging up in that area prior to the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not from his place anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there is basically just those three families to the west of you then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. AIRLIE NEIGHBORS

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then how about to the north, towards, what did you say, Staats or Stotts Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: North of us would be in Polk County.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Part of that is the School Forest now, and so, I'm interested in from your place most of the way to Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well, there was a fellow by the name of Doc Williams that owned a place up there, and the next one was Ace Staats, and the next one was a fellow by the name Moore. And then there was young Bill Williams and old Uncle Bill Williams. Old Uncle Bill weighed about 400 pounds I think. He had a little old pool hall down at Airlie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He had a pool hall in Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. He'd let us kids go down and play pool at noon, now and then anyway. He was quite an old character. He'd lived there for a long time. I remember one day we was down there and he was talking about a deer had came down. He says, "Forgot to go back."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The deer forgot to go back! [Laughs] Would. . . when you said that you did things for fun it was mostly hunting and fishing or visiting with the neighbors, that was during prohibition. Was there any dancing or drinking or anything of that sort happening?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, nothing unusual. Anyway, I don't think. . . they didn't have a problem like they had up around Yamhill and like they was taking stuff into Portland. There probably was a little hooch made. A little hooch drank. No big problem though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would. . . was there ever dancing in the neighborhood? Would they have dances or picnics?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, they had a high school gym [Airlie] and some other buildings. And they had dances, and they had picnics in the summertime, played a little baseball, stuff like that, that you did out in the country when you didn't have anything else to do. Couldn't afford to run around in cars very much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you ever go to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never was at Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never? How about Tampico. Would you ever go over to Tampico to visit, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Tampico was just a schoolhouse. Oh, yeah, we would visit some people over there. I don't remember their names now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the, did you know the Glenders? Or the Marcks? Or the Wiles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Wiles had a pretty good sized place. Didn't know them. The Glenders and what was the other name?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Goviers? Dobrinins?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Browns?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Stanbaugh? Did you know them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Are you talking about the Browns that owned the Forest Hill [Forest Peak]?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I think so. I think it would be the same.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well we used to see them occasionally and visit with him out on the range or someplace. He eventually moved, sold out and moved down by Corvallis, I think.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: You never have discussed that place that was. . . well, when I was teaching school there, the Whites. Now what place was that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Cornutts lived there when I first moved here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Is that the old Cornutt place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Way out where Cornutts lived. Forest Tandy lived down the creek. Forest kept a few cows along. He and I hunted and fished together quite a bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind offish would you catch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cutthroats. All the creeks there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it all cutthroats?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all I ever saw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you don't ever recall seeing any rainbow in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Oh, they were strictly native, they weren't planted. And they were darned good eating fish too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big would they get?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you'd catch them 7-8 inches up to a foot long. Mostly 10 or 11 inches is as big as they got. An 11" cutthroat and three or four of them makes you a pretty good meal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many could you catch in a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the limit was 30 when we went up there. I never caught more than 22. I probably could have come up with 30 if I'd have kept fishing. We were kind of conservationists, it went through our place, we'd go down and catch enough for a mess to eat. Maybe a few days later we'd catch another mess. We weren't trying to harvest all of them. And another thing about fish in them days, if you went down there and somebody that you didn't know would come along fishing, and you got up to him and visited with him a little and left him four or five holes to fish in and went on and fished down below. It's not that way these days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you fish in any creeks besides Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I used to fish Soap Creek once in a while. Soap Creek was a little bit harder to fish, but it had bigger fish in it. If you got 'em to bite we had some nice fish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Staats or Savage Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Savage Creek I never was able to catch many fish out of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was always the story about that great big fish that you had in the pond there behind your dam that you irrigated out of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Behind our dam?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah in that little pond that you had that you irrigated out of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For irrigation? Oh, we used to catch a few.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was always a story about a great big one in there that nobody could catch.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember who told that. We used to catch three or four that was a foot long out of there later in the summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you went to school, was that nine months a year?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it was 8 months and a half, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you went to grade school right there at the Berry Creek School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The end of the 7th grade and the 8th grade. Then I went to Airlie to high school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the local high school was at Airlie then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then, do you know how long that high school had been at Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A long time, but I don't know how long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the main town for the Berry Creek community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you had...

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I taught school there, too. After I left Berry Creek. Yes, I taught there for two years. I was teaching there when we got back.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Post Office was at Suver to start with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Post Office was at Suver? And then, the pool hall and the high school were at Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And there was a little country store down there that belonged to Johnny Weinert.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Weinert had the store at Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Post Office was in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they did move the Post Office from Suver to Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was a post office at Airlie and one at Suver. The one at Suver, though, was where they carried the mail from to deliver to your box. Then they moved it to Monmouth later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What other businesses were there at Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all the business I recall in particular. Over at Lewisburg . . . which is that Lewisville or Lewisburg over . . .? Levisville, I guess over by the Luckiamute River? There was a blacksmith's shop over there. Oh, I said there wasn't anything else. Johnny Weinert sold gas. And they sold gas over at Lewisville.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Weinert ended up with Coote's, what, third mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Weinert took over Coote's second mill when Coote and Cornutt got so badly in debt. All they had to do was to take over, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when did Coote form a partnership with Cornutt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, that would have been 1929 or sometime like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, right from the very start.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They were brother-in-laws.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who did the logging '

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean out in the woods?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, a fellow by the name of Burbank. My dad. And Forest Tandy. And, I don't know, maybe somebody else, but they were the main ones that I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, Tandy, and Dickey, and who was the other person?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Burbank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Burbank? Those were all local people, so the local fai.t were logging for the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Burbank wasn't a local farmer, he was a logger. There were two Burbanks, there was Pete Burbank which was the son, and I don't remember the old man's

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: d there. Yoncalla, I think. Was Yoncalla where Tandy from?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: That's where he went to I think. I don't know whether.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, he came from there and went back to Yoncalla.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I think that he logged down there, but I'm not sure. He may have run sheep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Burbanks, there's a great big tribe of them over at Pedee right now and they're all descended from the Burbank he's talking about.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Pete, and was Pete's brother named Chip?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I couldn't tell you the names of the older generation. I know the younger generation, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the Burbanks came in pretty much as contract loggers, to log?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He just came in to log, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He died pretty young, didn't he the one that was logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg your pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Didn't the Burbank that was logging die pretty young?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had logging teams. They just logged.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, but I mean, he had a heart attack or something when he was pretty young, like 45 or something, didn't he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Which one? Pete?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Pete was the youngest.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: There is another thing that you told me the other day, because Dorothy Johnson, said that [Unintelligible] and that Jack, her son had gone to school there [Berry Creek] and his sister did. Now, Jack's been dead a long time, but his sister, this one sister that she was mentioning is alive and could tell you about that. And I said Dorothy, I don't think so, I had them in school, I had Lucille when I was teaching school in Airlie, and as far as I knew they lived at Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Hauges lived in where Joe Smith's house was.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: And Don said, when I said this, he said, she's right, they were there before the Dickeys moved in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They weren't there when we were there. But they had been there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: No, they had moved on to Airlie by that time. But they did live in Berry Creek. So this Joe Smith house, that's that house that's still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's still there and a thousand people had lived in it I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it was always called the Joe Smith place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Far as I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Well, are you ready to take a break then and have some lunch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 7. FAMILY STORIES

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, well why don't we start with the story on your dad.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I was still in grade school down at Yamhill, why, my dad had a brother that lived at Sheridan, and a sister that lived over at Salem, and there was some other people that were cousins or something or another. Anyway, we all met up at Sheridan at his brother's. And we were going out to the old homestead. His folks' homestead. We got out to the fence, and here was a big apple tree there. And I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: don't remember what my dad said he did, but he said that's the only licking they ever got under the apple tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Only what?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the only licking he ever got was something he did under the apple tree and he wasn't supposed to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what it was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember now. Story sort of tickled me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that apple tree still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Tell him about the time he ate all the peaches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh ho. Well, dad and the neighbor down at Yamhill would go over to Carlton, or towards Carlton to pick peaches for canning. They liked a variety called muir, M-U-I-R. They were yellow peaches and they were a good flavor. So he and this neighbor were always competing to see which one could eat the most or pitch the most hay or something or another. So dad came home and he got sick and the neighbor, Bill Hankins, said he didn't wonder it, he said he ate 40 peaches. And what they'd eat was these ones that fell off the tree on the ground. And they were richer than anything. I much doubt if he ate 40 peaches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He ate enough to get sick though.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what the neighbor said.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And, when we interrupted before lunch there, we were talking about the people logging in the neighborhood. The different groups of people that were logging, and your dad was one group, or one logger, and Tandy was another logger, and there was a couple contract loggers, two brothers, Burbank.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At lunch we were talking a little bit about the religious affiliations of the people in the community. And the Burbanks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Burbanks apparently weren't real religious. In as far as I can remember. They were nice people, but I don't remember them showing up for Sunday school on a Sunday morning.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did most of the community go to the same church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there wasn't a church, really. What they had was a Sunday school every now and then over at the local. Berry Creek school. Or if they went to church they went to

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Airlie, which wasn't a very big church. They, I wouldn't say they were real religious people, but they were not anti-religious either, I mean, if a minister would come in and conduct some services most of 'em would show up. Except this one old boy [Perkins] that made the comments about that gopher being as ugly as he was or something like that. I don't think I ever saw him go to Sunday school.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 8. MILL WORKERS

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had a Sunday School then at the school, and then they had a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, every now and then. Sometimes it didn't last very long and sometimes it would last six months or a year or some traveling minister or something would stop by and start up a Sunday school. Oh, like Neil and his brothers and sisters and dad and mother and my dad and mother and my brother and I and, oh some of the other people that lived around the mill, there were quite a lot of people that lived in mill shacks around the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was going right towards our next question. In the mill shacks there was one of the Tandys, Matthew, and the Becks, do you remember those families?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Tandys or the Becks that lived in the mill shacks there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Tandys didn't live in mill shacks. Becks lived in them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was, I think Elmer did or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Elmer and his mother lived in a cabin down by Forest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Forest's cousin lived in a mill shack down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marty, I think his name was.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he lived in a mill shack. He was another mill worker that drifted around jobbed here and there. What was his name?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Alvie. A-L-V-I-E.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was quite a hunter. He and I went out on a coon hunt one night and we got a coon over on Folks Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you ever remember any stories of rattlesnakes on Folks Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think there was any rattlesnakes over there. We used to hunt graydiggers over there in the spring. And I never saw a rattlesnake.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of any?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. On the mill shacks. Were those only built when they put the mills in? Were there any people living there or any homes there before the mills came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No they weren't put in untill the mill was put in. There was no place to live, they'd come along, they'd get some of that side cut lumber and "salmon up" a shack and move in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any of the local people work in the mills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, . . some of the young fellows particularly. But, well I worked in .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Weinert's sawmill one summer. And a couple of friends of mine that went to school over in Airlie worked there the same summer. We had a sawyer that was building homes. He was logging, oh I think 20-28 feet logs, or 24 foot, something like that. They were only about so big.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About 20 inches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I doubt if they were more than 18. Sixteen to 18. And this old sawyer he'd ram her through and bang. And we cut over 200 logs a day some days. And one day this friend from Airlie was riding carriage and sitting, oh what do you call that [setting ratchets: NV], anyway he moved when the sawyer got back to where he wanted it, why he'd two fingers or one finger or whatever fit, the guy would work the lever to get it back real fast. And the old sawyer he got in a hurry. Boy, I thought my friend was going right into the saws but he didn't. Sort of scared the sawyer. He slowed down after that. There was another young fellow, he was from around there someplace, but he wasn't really local. He was . . ., no I was off-bearer, right behind the saw, and he [Edgar] ran the other saws to cut the timber up into 2x4's or whatever. And very frequently we would have 1000 feet of lumber piled over on work horses. We'd get caught up and we had to have a new log come in. And they had a guy out on the pond that didn't give you much time. They were really putting lumber out that summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the same pond that Neil said the flume came down to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this was another pond at the new mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they built two ponds on Savage Creek there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, one of them wasn't on Savage Creek, it was over on the side of the hill. And, that second mill, it wasn't too big a pond, it was big enough to hold all the logs they needed at the time but they hauled the logs in either on a dirt road or part of it was, well they put lumber and slabs on it and made a sort of a slab road and haul the lumber in on that. They haul 1000 or 2000 feet at a time on an old Ford truck or something of that sort.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call that, slab road, or.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tram road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Tram road, probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or corduroy?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tram road is what we called them. They were two 4x12's nailed side by side on a bunch of cross rails.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those were tram roads but without the metal rails?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, there was no rails.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did a lot of those around the country. Lumber was cheap.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was tram roads on Soap Creek, but I always thought they were the type with the metal rails. They call them plank roads or corduroy roads in different areas of the country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Corduroy roads the planks were crosswise. Tram roads they went lenght wide.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These tram roads saved bringing out dirt. I mean, if you had to level up an area you put some logs on top and your 4x10's or whatever they were and then your slabs across lengthways on it and make a road pretty fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, the mill would be cutting up the logs and then taking some of the lumber back out and constructing roads in the new areas.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they were burning slab. Slabs were sort of a waste product.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's what they used for the roads.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what they used for the roads, ordinarily.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they burn the stuff up in wigwam burners, or just out in open fires?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Usually they just had open fires, didn't they Neil?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Becks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Becks? Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maxine can probably tell you more about them. Do you want to tell him?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I did. [Had talked about the Becks at lunch.]
bracketed_corrections: [Had talked about the Becks at lunch.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh. Yeah, he was real religious, I think, because he didn't have to work when he got religious. And he'd go to Klamath Falls or someplace or another, leave the family there and get by the best they could. And there were three or four kids and Mrs. Beck. They were pretty nice family, actually, but the old man ought to have had his teeth taped together a time or two.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I understand that Mrs. Forest Tandy and your mother sometimes had to help feed some of the families in the neighborhood.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably did, I don't remember off hand. I know Mrs. Tandy did, and we had apples and stuff we gave them. And Mabel Tandy, Forest's wife, had a heart as big as the moon

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: There was a cute story about that. And I say this to him every now and then.
