But whenever Forest got ranting about something you know, or was having some kind of trouble, he was complaining, she'd look at him and say, "Do you think you'll ever amount to anything Tandy?" And this usually calmed him down. So I say that to him sometimes. "Think you'll ever amount to anything Dickey?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Rate I'm going now, I don't think so. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: This is a story about Mabel. And she had, she was legally blind. You know, across the room she could not count how many fingers you held up. So she had her knives painted red, the handles, so she could.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Elmer Tandy, Forest's brother, was sawyer quite a while there. He and his mother lived in a little house down by Forest, down there, maybe it was the next place. Anyway, until Elmer decided to go to. . . he got married and decided to go to another mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, how long had the Tandy's lived there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they moved there after we did. I think Forest had owned the 60 acres for quite a while but I suppose they moved there in 1930 or something like that. And I think they were still there when the cantonement took over weren't they?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I guess.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, in 1942.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 9. BUNDLING AND HOP PICKING

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yes. They were there when I was teaching school, because I boarded with them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a Mr. Withrow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Witlow?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Withrow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Withrow?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We drove bundle wagons for him.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Harold Withrow, he was a farmer and had a dairy farm and he ran a threshing machine in the summer time. And the locals, well Tandy and my dad, and I and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I drove bundle wagons for him, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know Neil drove bundle wagon for him. One summer they were starting to raise hairy vetch and rye grass and I don't know whether you've ever had any experience farming or not?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway this hairy vetch was just one big mess. I mean, it was fluffy and you couldn't pitch the hay, I couldn't pitch it in the machine fast enough to keep the sack sower busy, and anyway we spent most of the summer doing that, and one day Forest came around to me and says "The next field we're going to is wheat." And he says "It's in short bundles. Thought maybe I was gonna make it first, but I guess I'm not." But he says "You're gonna be the first load there so get a good big load of the short bundles and when you get into the machine work that sack sewer so that he can hardly keep up with it." Well I did that except the sock sewer lost his needle. And Withrow was pretty proud of this old thrashing machine. And he told me that only one guy had ever been able to plug the thing up and his name was Tommy . . . well,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: he lived down by Joe Smith, and he was young fellow, probably in college and well built. One day I got in there and Withrow was setting out on the sack pile, and I started in getting bundles placed out in front and kept adding to them and pretty quick I got down to where hay was full and then I started pitching them. Pretty quick it goes "whrr, rrr, rrr," Old Withrow he was a signaling me to slow down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was there when you did that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I beg your pardon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was there. I still remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Neil told me that story a couple of weeks ago. Must have been pretty impressive.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, actually, the old machine wasn't as good as it had been before, so maybe I wouldn't have been able to do it. I was not too slow, I worked on a farm and pitched hay and bundled and cut wood and stuff, so I had pretty good muscles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that your first job?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no. My first job was picking prunes when I was about 6 years old. I was down at Yamhill at that time. I made a dollar the first day I worked. I got 12 cents a box that year. Then, from then on I picked prunes or picked hops or something every summer. We just needed the money so we could buy books and go to school. I mean, kids worked in those days, they didn't sit around and watch TV and say, "Ma, what can we do next?" I think it was good for them. They didn't . . . nobody got hurt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you pick hops for Branches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I picked hops down at Mike Branches, and .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, we picked for Branches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We picked down at Millers. Was it Millers down the road? Well, anyway, dad bossed hop yards part of the time. And we picked hops. Anything in the fall or summer to make a few bucks so we had enough money to buy books and clothes and stuff, because there wasn't any free money those days. No government programs. You made your money or you didn't make it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: His mother picked with him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The baskets that they picked hops in were about that big around and that tall. You had 25 cents when you got one full.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much can you make in a day picking hops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If I had a good v, I made 2 bucks.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 10. FALLING AND BUCKING

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much working in the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think I got 3 and a half a day that summer. This was getting up toward when things began to pick up. Probably about '37 or sometime about then, and wages had begun to increase a little bit. Then, in '38 I worked in the sawmill and I got a job when they slowed it down at Weinert, I got a job for Cooper bucking logs, short logs. And I think we made 3.25 a day to start with, the' ring when we'd have a little timber of our own and dad wanted to c cut that before I ..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: went back to Cooper. And I got 3.50 when I went back but I was the only bucker there then. In the fall, why, old Hap came out one day and watched me. He had, there was two of us bucking and then they had another guy down at the sawmill that was bigger than I was and he wanted me to. . . he was pond monkey.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did the pond monkey do?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Put logs into the mill from the pond. He wanted to know if I didn't want to change jobs with this guy. That was McCoy.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: That was who?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: McCoy.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Oh, Cary, the old man?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cary Mccoy, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he wasn't noted for being real ambitious.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He sure made a lot of kids.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I said no, I don't want any part of that stuff on the pond. And old Hap, he was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: gonna show me how to buck logs. Pretty quick he about rolled a log on me, so he went back to the mill and left me alone. So, a few weeks later, why, we were bucking small logs again, made ties and that stuff, mostly. So he came out one night with this other fellow from Independence, he was a big long guy, he was a good worker but he just didn't move too fast. He said, "Well, how many logs did you get

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: today?" and he kinda grinned. I said "72, why?" His face got about a foot long. He says, "I thought sure I'd beat you. I only got 70." He was a good worker. But actually, if it had been big logs he could probably beat me. Small logs, why I could get down to the ground and saw 'em off pretty fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Donald's fairly short.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: 5 '3" in case you want to know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A lot of times that works better if you are working close to the ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then in the summer of '38 another fellow that was working for Hap at the time and I decided that we could make more money up west of Dallas and so we went up and got a job, he got a job falling and I got a job bucking. And I averaged 5 bucks a day up there. You had to furnish your own tools. And that was a buck and a half more than I was making down there. Some days I made 7 dollars a day which was pretty good money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of tools were you using to buck with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Seven foot bucking saws.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Swede fiddle.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The old, what did they call them, wire cutters or something of the sort. [Also called Misery Whip: NV]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you do to bump knots? What would you hit knots with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg your pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you knock the limbs off with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, an axe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you'd use an axe on the limbs and then a bucking saw to buck the lengths.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. If there was any sign of rot at all you'd long butt it. Do you know what long buttin' is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, but you want to explain it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You cut off the stuff that you think is rotten. And we had some stuff that was blue that they haul now and understand get extra money for it. We had to take almost the log length off of some of these trees. ["Log length" was 16 feet. Most Berry Creek "long butts" were 10 feet or less.] It was in a little spot up on top of the mountains. But it was a nice place to work. I worked there till the first of September, I guess,
bracketed_corrections: ["Log length" was 16 feet. Most Berry Creek "long butts" were 10 feet or less.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: when Hugh had, or we all moved someplace else as I remember. A fellow from Independence was doing the logging, and so I made pretty good money that summer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I had enough I went back to school. I could stay in school for the rest of four years. I started in '37 and got through to the spring of '38 and then I had to lay out '38 and '39. Started again in '39 and graduated in '42.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 11. OREGON STATE COLLEGE

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did you live while you were going to school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In Corvallis. I bached.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just by yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you live Just by yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, most of the time. Well, part of the time. Part of the time I had a roommate.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: He bached with Jake Frobe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I bached with Jake Frobe, I bached with Foster, then Lee and I finally, Lee Kuhn, have you met Lee Kuhn?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lee was a graduate student from Ohio, no Iowa. In Fish and Game. And he and I lived together. Well, from the first of January to the 21st of March, I guess. The old army was breathing down my neck and Maxine and I were gonna get married in June. So I went back spring term to register, and they notified me I was gonna be in the army pretty quick. Fortunately, I had worked on wildlife damaged farm crops the summer before, and I was continuing to do some work on it. So I went down to the draft board and I knew most of em, and told em what I was trying to do to get done and help the farmers out. Could I get a deferment to untill the end of the school

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: year. They didn't give me a deferment, they gave me something that was as good. Quick as the school year was out, I went up to Portland to take my physical. And they put me from 4A to FiB, I think it was. Then in the summer, why, they called me up again and the local doctor, Dr. Ball I think it was there in Corvallis, said "I'll take care of this for you." And I didn't know what he was talking about. He put me in some other classification, and the next three years I think we moved about 10 times. They finally quit acknowledging my change of address.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you trying to keep out of the service?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I wasn't trying to keep out. I was just working, doing a job. And I wanted to finish up this paper on damage to farm crops. What we was trying to do was to come up with a chemical that you could treat the seed with that would keep the pheasants from digging corn out, stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was for your thesis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just another paper. I didn't have to do a thesis for a bachelor's degree. And I didn't. I think I did four papers one term.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I had to type those.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's my typist over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Going back a little bit, to Berry Creek, we talked about picnics. And Maxine was saying that every year that they used to have a picnic at your pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pond?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That pond at your home there, did you have picnics there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no, we didn't have it there, we had it on the creek over on Savage Creek. Over by school. Where we had our pond, the cows ran, and it wasn't a very good place to have a picnic.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. So it was back by the log pond?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was down below the log pond a little ways. It was a real pretty spot there, trees, and shade, and this creek. Oh, sometimes there was some cattle in there, but no problem or stepping into things you didn't want to, that sort of thing. It was real pretty. We used to cut through across that place to go up, to come and go to school. And one spring I was going through there and all of a sudden down in the dead leaves ahead of me -- you asked me about rattlesnakes -- this old snake rattled in there and I went about 4 feet high I think. It was just a bull snake in there, I had startled him and he was rattling. There are a lot of bull snakes, they don't do any harm, they catch mice and insects and things. Far as I know, closest rattlesnakes are to that country is down here. Maybe some over by Falls City, I don't know. Out south of here on Spencers Butte and out on Coburg Hill, and some other places south of here there's quite a few rattlesnakes. I killed a whole bunch one spring with cyanide. The guy had already killed 63 between two flat rocks. They called me and I went out and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: used cyanide on them. I used it another year, and they didn't have any more complaints. I don't know whether I thinned them out or whether they just give up on it. They were on the south side of Spencers Butte. Well, and interesting story on that. The first summer I was out of college this other kid and I got a job and were working on young pheasants, 6 to, no 8-12 weeks when they released they wanted to know which ones age class was surviving the best. I was posted on a little island up in the Columbia River named McGuire's Island, about the north end of Government Island. Rather nice place to work. Hank Snyder, the other guy, was stationed down here in Eugene. He worked down here on Christiansen's farm. And that Spencer Butte out there is further on the northwest corner, I guess. Anyway, Hank went down one morning and Christiansen brothers were running this rodeo and stuff, and had some of these brahma bulls and stuff in there, and they were always giving Hank a bad time about being tackled by a brahma bull or something. And Hank couldn't tell whether they were kidding him or not. And anyway, this one morning, they said to Hank "Say, are you running around in that tall grass over by the Creek, looking for dead birds and stuff'?" Hank said, "Yeah, why?" They said, "You want to be careful doing that at this time of the year, the rattlesnakes move down off of Spencers Butte." Well Hank was raised in Kansas, he hadn't seen any rattlesnakes. He thought they were pulling his leg again. And that afternoon he darned near stepped on one. And he and the boss were down on McGuire Island a day or two later and telling about it. Boss says, "You ought to see old Hank now. He steps about 4 feet high and about 4 feet long."

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 12. BERRY CREEK STORIES

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember Bob Wilt? Or the Dobrinins?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How do you spell that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: W-I-L-T?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Whereabouts? Berry Creek, or. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Parkers? Do you remember the Parkers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived over by the sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In one of the mill shacks there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Bob Wilt, I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember about the Parkers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they had a family, three or four or five kids, he was another one of these mill workers, and worked enough to make a living if he had to. And the kids had sort of a rough time. They went to school, didn't one of the Parker girls go to school to you?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yes, Emma Parker went to school to me and her two younger brothers. Henry, who was called Buck, and Amel, who was about 2nd grade.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Unintelligible] another mill shack family that went to school there and worked when he had to, when the mill was working. He wasn't known for a huge amount of ambition.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would the local farm families think about having mills in there and having these mill worker families in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Didn't bother them. They knew that well this was in the '30's. And everybody . . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was having a rough time. Didn't make any difference whether you were a farm family or. . . even Joe Smith was having a rough time with his 1000 acres of good soil.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about McAlpine? Where did you meet him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: McAlpine?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Les was in the same grade in high school as I was. He had been over at Airlie, and his dad got a tree fell on him up there in the woods. This is something that I wouldn't want to go in a story, but supposedly .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Should I shut this off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we can say he was killed by a falling tree, though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg your pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was killed in a logging accident. Les McAlpine.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was a logger.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old was he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he was around 60 I guess, when it happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a place called Kozy Nook Egg Farm? On Statts Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Say it again?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kozy Nook Egg Farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cozy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nook. Egg Farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Farm?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Egg Farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where was it supposed to be?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it was down Statts Creek about 2 miles north of your place, on the west side of Statts Creek, kind of up in the hills there a little bit.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think anybody called that Statts Creek. Do you know where Statts Creek is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's just a creek down through the brush and reeds and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it would start draining off the back side of your house there. That was the kind of headwaters of it, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well. . . yeah I suppose so. In fact, we lived up in the middle of the farm and there was a ditch. A ditch ran down through there and emptied in to what was Statt's Creek, I guess. Kozy Nook Farm -- Well, Cox's lived down there and they didn't call it Kozy Nook Farm. And it was the only ranch down there, really. I mean there was Carl Hauge's ranch, and this Green's place, but I don't think either one of them called the place Kozy Nook.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you remember any stories from Tampico? Any stories about what kind of community that was, or anything at all about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was just another farm community, I don't remember any particular stories. When they closed the school at Berry Creek my brother hauled the kids from Berry Creek over to Tampico to go to school for a couple of years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about the ghost town that used to be there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't even know there was a town there untill today.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. Do you recall any stories about any gold mines, or stolen gold, or buried gold in the Berry Creek or Soap Creek area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never heard of any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If there was anything my dad would've known about it because he sure had a nose for gold.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think anybody had enough money to bury dollar gold pieces.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think this goes back to the gold rush in 1850's when the stages used to run through the area. Jim Hanish mentioned, and maybe you don't want this on the tape, but he mentioned something that between your families living next door there was kind of a feud between the two of them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no feud. [Text Deleted]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He'd [Hanish] get in trouble with everybody.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'll have to tell you a little bit about that. I was over at Hanish's when the Dickeys were cutting the logs for their barn, and anyway, they were over there and they'd fall a tree and they'd holler "TIMBER". And old man Hanish he says, "They ought to say 'BRUSH'." Did you ever work for Hanish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever work for Hanish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wouldn't work for him if I was starving to death.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. There was three mills that we've talked about. Coote had three mills, and the Cooper brothers, and Bennett brothers. Do you recall any other mills in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, in the neighborhood was Cooper's and Coote and Cornutt and Bennett Brothers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that called Coote and Cornutt, is that how they called the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Coote and Cornutt, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And Coote and Cornutt and Cooper came in about the same time, and Bennett Brothers about the mid '30's. And they had just a little mill, that mostly they ran, these two brothers, mostly I think they ran by themselves with one other man.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they power those mills? What kind of power did they use on them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Steam, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All three of them?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bennett's had an Allis Chalmers motor on his.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, Bennett's probably didn't have steam. I'm not sure that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I worked for Bennett Brothers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh did you? I'm not sure that Cooper's had steam, I think that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was a lot of whistles blowing at 5.00.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cornutt and Coote had steam.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of person was Coote?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Coote?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh Bill was a nice guy. Had quite a bit of ambition, but I don't think he was the best manager in the world. But he did develop, after he got out of the mill there, he did develop a little portable mill wasn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I lost track of Bill Coote after that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he moved down to California and I think he was building and selling portable mills and doing pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ah hah. How about Cornutt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He went to a prune farm over by Monmouth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh did he?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh. I didn't know what happened to him. He had four sons, I think. And I never

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I lost track of them. His mother lived to be 100 years old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cornutt's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She lived with her daughter, Thursa Coote. And back in those days, you didn't get wine unless you had something . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're talking about uh. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mrs. Cornutt who lived to be over 100 years old. She had some kind of a problem where a glass of wine helped. She had a glass of wine every day. And this was during prohibition days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would she get the wine?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that you could buy it with a permit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. So she had kind of like a medical permit, or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think so. I mean she wasn't a lady to go out and get drunk or anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was something that whatever her problem was, it helped her out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the Cootes and Cornutts looked upon as pretty solid members of the community? Did most people get along with them real well?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, they were good solid members of the community.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, I understand that Weinert ended up owning Coote's third mill. Do you know the story behind that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would be his second mill I think. But anyway it was the one around the side of the mountain. Well, Coote was paying off his help with groceries and stuff, that he bought from Weinert. And finally it just got to the point that Johnny sat down with the bill and they decided that Johnny should take the mill over and go from there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then, is that when Coote went down to California at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that's when he went to California.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did Weinert keep the mill going then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Weinert had the mill up there going a couple of years or whatever it took to cut the timber off. Then he had a mill over on his own place, over on Weinert Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Weinert Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You know, that I said that the Weinert farm was over the hill west of the Hauge farm where Coopers mill was?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that Weinert had a mill over there. Cooper had a mill over there too. But

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not sure whether Weinert did or not. But anyway there was a mill over there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 13. FOREST FIRES AND REFORESTATION

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any forest fires in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any forest fires in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only forest fire that I ever remember was one spring that they wanted to burn some stuff off before it got too dry and they set it afire and it took off and they had to, my dad had to fight fire, it was about 6:00 before they got it out so they could come home and eat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a very big fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't know. Two acres?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that is the only fire you can remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the only fire I ever remember. I don't know why they didn't have a good fire up there. Had plenty of logging and stuff. They'd burn that. They'd go in there quick as it started to rain the fall and set it afire and burn it up while it was still raining.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The slash?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The slash, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they ever plant trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They left seed trees in those days. Something that they're missing out on now, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the seed trees work?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You're darn right they work. Interesting sidelight to this, is that in 1957 after the College had a bunch of this timber land up there, they called me up one day and says "Hey, what do you know about doing wood rat control?" This was a bushy footed wood rat, I think. I says I don't know anything about it, but I'll look it up in books and see. I was doing rat control and rabbit control, and all those things, but we hadn't run into wood rat problems. So I says, why don't I come up and talk to you and see what your problem is and we'll see what we can work out. So I went up and talked to the fellow, and he took us out and showed us around, and they had discovered there on the, oh what did he call that, up there that College forest to start with?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Adair tract? Or McDonald Forest? Dunn.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, McDonald or whatever. Anyway, they were losing 45% of their trees or something like that, but it was a heck of a bunch of them. So I says, well, I'll look

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: up and see what I can find out in the literature and let you know. But I couldn't find out anything about doing wood rat control. So I called him up and told him, I says, "Now, if you want us to do something, we will spend some time up there seeing what we can come up with. And then if we come up with something that will work, why, we'd like to do the work for you." Well he says "That's fine." So we spent a couple of weeks up there trying out different things, and finally we found out that Thallium sulfate on grain did a job. Thallium sulphate's a bad word now, but it wasn't then. So he says, "Well how much will it cost to get this problem under control?" And I says, "Well, when you are talking about how much, do you want us to charge by the acre, or how?" And he said, "Well, yeah, I suppose by the acre would be a good way." So I said, "Let us do 40 acres for you and then figure out how much time it takes, what it'd take for us to break even or a little better on our wages, on the thing." So we did 700 acres of wood rat control for him the next two or three months. Got 3 bucks an acre for doing it. And we were the only ones doing it. We were the only ones that knew much about wood rat control for a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who were you dealing with at the school there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg your pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who was the man you were dealing with at the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was trying to remember his name a while ago. He was a forester up there, I can't remember his name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it be Nettleton or Rowley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nettleton or Rowley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nettleton, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He isn't still around is he?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nettleton was a good guy. We was out one day and he was telling me about one time when he was younger they were out, and had to camp overnight or something. Anyway, they sent him out to get some dry wood to burn. And he found a, oh these trees that lose their needles in the wintertime [Larch}? He found one of those and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was sure he had a dry tree so he cut it down. He laughed about it. Yeah, Nettleton, he was a nice guy. But that was kind of interesting. All that wood rat damage was out on land that they, Smith and -- or Coote and Cornutt logged first. And part of it was over on McDonald Forest and we, I had one man that worked out continuously, then I helped when I could get away from what I was doing down in Eugene. We worked out baits for several different animals, helped the farmers and the timber men or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's rabbits in that neighborhood. Did you ever see any unusual type of rabbits around the Forest Peak area? Up around Berry Creek at the higher elevations?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were jack rabbits and marsh rabbits and there could have been some snowshoes. But I don't know for sure about the snowshoes.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 14. BENNETT BROTHERS MILL

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. On the Bennett Brothers mill. Do you remember anything about the Bennett Brothers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Only that it was up there for three or four years or something like that. Neil can probably tell you more about Bennett Brothers than I can.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember them personally?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh Bennett Brothers? Yeah, they were pretty good workers. I think they worked for somebody else when they came in there, then they went to work and built their own mill and worked for themselves. I think they only put out maybe 5 or 6 thousand feet a day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Actually, I hauled slab wood for them, for Jack Green.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beg you pardon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I hauled slab wood out to the road for Jack Green out of their mill. I got about two cords a day.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They weren't a gung ho outfit. They probably made a living for themselves, which is probably what they intended to do to start with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they live in that neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they lived . . . by that time, Johnny Cornutt had moved away from the house across the road where he lived in, and at least one of the Bennetts and his wife lived there. I don't know where the other one lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mentioned knowing Charlie Olson. Can you tell me that story again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean the one about the cows?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You want me to go over it again for you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, we didn't record it last time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or you can tell me a different story, if you like.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's the only one I really know about. Charlie came over there one day, I guess along in February, it was pretty late for the cows to still be running on pasture. Well, I think they were steers, mainly. Three or four of them. Anyway, they had gotten into Hanish's 40 acres over there. I don't know whether Hanish didn't know they were there or what, but anyway, Charlie come over and said to me, he says, "Hey, I got a problem." He says, "I got, I think it's four steers, they're over at old man Hanish's place." And he says, "I'm a little bit afraid to go over and get 'em." I says, "Why?" "Well, he's kind of unpredictable." I said, "Well I guess you're right, there." So I said, "Well, let's go take a look at them." Well Hanish was over on across the creek on the other side doing something. These cows were right by a gate by our place, or steers, I said I don't see any problem here, we'll just open the gate, run them through, and close the gate while Hanish is across the creek. So that's the way we did it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he even see you? Hanish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so. I suppose he figured out what happened to it. But I wouldn't have cared if he had caught me at taking them out, cause he would have [Unintelligible] they'd have been a little afraid of Charlie Olson, watching there, the whole thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you know about Charlie? Did you know much about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Charlie was, I think he was Swedish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he and his wife used to come over once in a while. She was a real nice person. I think they were from Sweden, but outside of that we, he had oh I guess a few acres of hay over there and a dozen or so head of cattle that he ran in the summer, and I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: don't know whether he milked cows or whether he raised them for beef and sold them. He was over quite a ways from where we were, but we knew him because he used to come through checking, had we seen his cows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know any of the people on the Soap Creek side very well at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I knew some names but I didn't know the people very well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Cooper brothers, when they put their mill in there, did they live in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived at Airlie. Hap was the older brother and Frank was the younger one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there would have been Weinert's mill, Coote's and Cornutt's mills, Cooper Brothers and Bennett Brothers, is that the only four mill owners then in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Far as I know. That is real local. They used to tell a story on Hap Cooper. Hap had quite a temper you see. And he had one of these about 5 gallon fir barrels that they had nails in that was empty that they used for sitting on at lunch. And something went wrong at lunch why he'd come through and kick that empty 5 gallon wooden container about twice or three times. So these honory so-and-so's filled the thing part full of nails one day. He came through and kicked it that day before he discovered it had nails in it. I guess that cured him of kicking barrels.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 15. CAMP ADAIR

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When Adair came in, there were these mills in the neighborhood, and then there was farmers in the neighborhood, mostly subsistence farmers, and then there was the mill workers and the shacks and maybe a few other families in the neighborhood. But then Adair came in and started purchasing properties. What was the general feeling of those different groups of people about selling their land?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They didn't have any choice. They knew it. They just sold out and bought another place somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were people bitter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were people upset?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, not particularly, I don't think. Was your folks upset?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We got moved out before Camp Adair by a year. The Federal Land Bank moved us out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh. We got, had 160 acres, and I think we got $7200 for it. And we went over, the folks went over by Wren and bought a place from a fellow over there that had 180 acres. And I think they got it for $7200. So it wasn't too bad. Back in the '40's, why, we went out to help people and show them how to get rid of moles. And went down to Deadwood creek, and only three fellows showed up for the demonstration. And...

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 16. RODENT CONTROL

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you working for Oregon State at that time, the &tension Service.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I was working for myself, but I cooperated with Oregon State and if they needed a demonstration on mole control or gopher control or whatever, I'd go do it for 'em. And in turn they helped sell bait for me. And so it was a cooperative deal, I mean, we understood each other. I wasn't taking advantage of them and they weren't taking advantage of me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know a man named Hooven?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hooven?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hoover?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hooven.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hooven, oh Ed Hooven?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Ed and I worked together, he worked for the Forestry, State Forestry Department. Lee Kuhn and I worked together, Lee Kuhn was the fish and game guy that I mentioned a while ago. [Woman looks in around curtain enclosure towards Don.] That was my daughter just snuck around here. Anyway, about '45 they wanted me to come down to Deadwood Creek. There were three fellows showed up. One of them was sort of a younger fellow. So I showed them how to set traps and stuff, and what we knew how to tell them for sure. This young guy stood there and looked at me and then he says "Jesus Christ, you sons of bitches have been telling us that for 10 years!" I decided that was about time for somebody to start to work on a mole bait. So I spent 7 years working out a mole bait, trying I don't know how many different things. Finally I got one that worked and I just tried to register it in Oregon
bracketed_corrections: [Woman looks in around curtain enclosure towards Don.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and Washington wanted some, got it from them, or they got it up there somehow or another, and then recently, well, for the last 10 years or so, they've been trying to get registered nationally to the EPA. And the old EPA has been hard to get along with. And finally they had a request from Wisconsin or Michigan or someplace back there to get the mole bait to try out, and it worked like a charm. And also, it worked down in Missouri where my great grandfather homesteaded, because I took some down to a fellow that lives there, and he came back out he was wanting more to take back. Anyway, they came out with a report that, how good this mole bait was that he had tried out [Unintelligible], and so immediately the EPA called up Doug [Freeman] and says "Hey, why don't you get that mole bait registered." I don't know how I had enough guts to do that. Anyway, it came that this is considered one of the number one mole baits in the country. And I spent a long time working on it and checking on it, so I feel pretty good about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you started what, in '45 on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: '45 and got it to where I was willing to register it in '52. Seven years. Still it's looking pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it still hasn't been registered even now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they're registering it now. Nationally, they'll be able to sell all over the country as quick as they get it registered with the EPA and other states.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have the patent on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I sold it to Doug and I had to sell him the stuff that would make a patent on it. Anyway, I'm too old to manufacture mole bait anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, say Don, one thing that came to mind, when you were doing rodent control, did you work with any of the rodents in the Tillamook Burn, in their reforestation program?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In where?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In the Tillamook Burn in that reforestation program? They were having a problem with mice on that.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: On the Tillamook Burn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no Ed Hooven did that work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just Ed Hooven did it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were working on the white footed mice on that.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 17. MAXINE

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then on Camp Adair, when your family moved out, did you talk to any of the families in that neighborhood since that time, did you talk with Gerald McKibbon, or any of those families that stayed in the neighborhood around Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Which one, McKibbon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Maxine boarded at McKibbon's when she taught school at Airlie. So we'd see them at the Airlie-Lewisville picnic almost every year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did the families think about having Adair right next door during the war?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they didn't seem to resent it that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, when the families had to move out, they were kind of resigned to it, they weren't bitter or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never heard any saying that they resented it. I mean, there was a war going on. And the Japs were crowding the west coast. And we didn't want them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were kind of doing your part in a lot of ways.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we would just as soon grab the old 30-30 and sit up on a cliff and pick them off one at a time if we had a chance.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, after the war was over, and you had an opportunity to buy your land back, did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I apparently didn't. Mother probably could have, except she didn't want it. I went and asked about buying it and they said no, that the College had already put in for it. So maybe I couldn't, I don't know. Anyway, I would have liked to have the place back, we had it in pretty good shape. It wasn't the best land in the country but it produced pretty good pasture and it had some possibilities out there. One thing, there was good deer hunting out there. And good fishing. On that little creek. If they'd said I could have it for $5,000 I'd have tried to come up with it. I don't know .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: one of the people out there, Gil Innis, didn't sell his property, at least this is what I understand, he kept it and leased it to them. So when they were through with it why he just went back to farming it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You liked that land then pretty much in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's not the best land in the country, but it was not the worst either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those pretty enjoyable years, the years you lived on Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I enjoyed them. We had a $210 payment that was due on the place every fall. That was sometimes a worry. And then the taxes was $47 dollars or something like that. And we were getting the place paid for and, oh, we had a good herd of cows, milk, cream, wasn't too bad, and dad raised hogs on the skimmed milk and sold them, except one or two we butchered for ourselves. Mother raised turkeys a year or two. All in all we had a good time up there, I mean it was a rough time all over the country, but the neighbors were all in the same shape we were, and we visited and shared things together like apples that we had that they didn't have. Hunted and fished together, and all in all I'd say it was one of the better times I enjoyed my whole life before I was married.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Thank you for adding that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you meet your wife?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She made a mistake and came down from Portland to teach school at Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what year?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And do you remember when you first met?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, not too long after she got there. But we didn't do anything about it till the next spring, she came up one night and my mother was cool towards her I think. She came up one night to get something, and I came in from work and she was standing there talking to mother. And she said "Well, I guess I better get going." As I recall, mother invited her to stay for dinner. And I said, "If you want to stay for dinner, I'll take you home afterwards." So I took her home down to Tandy's after we got through with dinner, and when she went back to Portland I didn't know whether she was going to be interested in me or not after that spring. The first thing I knew, I was baching, bucking logs over toward Monmouth. First thing I know here come in the mail a cookbook, how to cook. So she hooked me.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: He says he couldn't run fast enough to get away. That's not the way I did it. I have to tell you the story, because he tricked me. When he asked me to marry him, I said "Well, I won't marry you if you're going to be a farmer, because I don't want to live on a farm, I was not raised on a farm, I'm not a farm girl, I don't know how to be a farmer's wife and I don't want to."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Girl ought to know better than to believe you hadn't she?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: And he said, "Oh, i'm not going to be a farmer. No, I'm not gonna be a farmer." Well, we've got a 10 acre farm now. You know, he tricked me.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But she's still with me. We've been married for 48 years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 48 years.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Almost 49.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: We have three good kids. This one's our middle one. She lives across the mountains at Madras, and her husband is a doctor for the Indians on the Warm Springs Indian Reservation. And that's her oldest son, and then she has a little one besides, who is 8 years old, and is staying with his cousin. And then our oldest daughter lives here, and she's 45 now, is Diane gonna be 45 this year?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Diane? Yeah, she'll be 45.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah, she was born in '45, so she's gonna be 45 in '90. And that one is 41, I guess, and then the other son, Jim is 38, this last week.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In your life, what do you think has been the best part of your life?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Best part of my life?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The last 48 years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sounds like good politics and an honest answer, both.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we've got three wonderful kids and some great grandkids and we're real proud of them. Eric earned $3,000 to go to the scout jamboree back in Virginia last summer. And .

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [END OF RECORDING]

chapters.title: APPENDIX A: TRIBUTE TO MY FATHER
chapters.label: A

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: APPENDIX A: TRIBUTE TO MY FATHER

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Donald Dickey Eulogy read at funeral service, Trinity Methodist Church, Eugene, Oregon, October 2, 1990, by his daughter, Patricia

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: When my father was hospitalized in July, there was an evening that his physicians prepared the family for the possibility he wouldn't survive the night. The next morning, my mother's phone rang at about 8:00. She answered anxiously to hear a voice on the other end say, "This is Old Man Dickey reporting from Star Ship Earth. I wanted to let you know I'm still here."

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Both my parents related this anecdote to me, but my father added a sequel. He told me, with a mixture of pride and amazement, that, later that day, my mother had said he was the most remarkable man she had ever known.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: What made my father so remarkable was his strength of character. He lived by strong principles, and believed that the proper response to adversity was simply to pick yourself up, dust yourself off, and move on down the road.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: He was raised on a farm, where a childhood accident lead to osteomyelitis. This resulted in many weeks spent in the hospital, the loss of some bone from one leg, having to learn to walk again--which he always referred to as the hardest thing he ever had to do--and a permanent limp. His perpetual response when asked about the incident was a shrug of his shoulders--no big deal.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: In spite of his physical problems, he finished school and worked his way through Oregon State University. He married my mother in 1942. I once read that the greatest gift a man can give his children is to love their mother. My father lived by that principle.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: He gave us many other gifts as well--honesty, integrity, responsibility, a love of growing things, the freedom to be anything we chose, respect for education, and the strength to stand by our principles, whether in a crowd or alone.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: My father loved life. He had a wonderful sense of humor. He loved his family and his many close friends. The visits and cards he received during his illness lifted his spirits immensely. He had hopes of completing several projects around the farm--he envisioned a pond, a greenhouse and a workshop.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The most difficult question I ever asked my father was how he wanted to be remembered by his grandsons, Eric, Mark and Mikie. He thought a moment and said, "I want them to remember me as a good grandfather who loved them very much and hoped they will grow into good men."

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Old Man Dickey has filed his last report from Star Ship Earth. I wanted to let you know he will always be with us.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Patricia Dickey Creelman September 30, 1990

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: APPENDIX B: SCHOOL DAY MEMORIES

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Unfortunately, Don died of liver cancer before he saw the transcript of the interview with Bob Zybach. I had told him that Bob said the tape from the Care Center, in spite of the interruptions and background noises, had been better than Bob dared hope, and that Bob was pleased with it. Don told many people that he really enjoyed doing the interview and visiting with Neil Vanderburg after so many years. He was looking forward to seeing the book. I think Don felt pleased to have been able to contribute information to a worthwhile project. He had many contacts with Oregon State University during the years - helping out with rodent control problems, attending reunions and get-togethers with a number of life-long friends that had graduated with him in 1942. He even taught occasional classes in Rodent Control for Professor Lee Kuhn of the Fish & Game Department. Don and Lee were batching together at the time Don and I got married, and they remained best friends all these years.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I remember the first time I met Don. It was in 1938 when I went to apply for teacher at the Berry Creek School. His father was a member of the school board and his mother was the clerk. His younger brother, Kenneth, was checking out the prospective school-marm, but Don was in the dining room studying. At the time he was attending Oregon State.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Berry Creek was a typical one-room school with desks of assorted sizes and a huge wood- burning stove. In 1938 there were 14 pupils, scattered among eight grades: Dolores, Lloyd and Herbert Beck; Mildred Goodin; Donald Lewis; Mabel, Mary Jane, Melvin and Morris McCoy; Emil, Emma May and Henry Parker; Billy and Ruth Vanderburg. There were at least 10 McCoy children, all of whose first names began with "M". In 1939-40 only 10 children were enrolled: the three Becks, Don Lewis, the four McCoys, Billy Ennis and Wilfred Ray, who lived with Forrest and Mabel Tandy. I boarded with the Tandys and their daughter, Edith, who was in high school. High school students attended Corvallis High School. The bus driver was an Oregon State student who boarded at Vanderburgs. A non-denominational Sunday School met at the school house on Sunday morning, taught by Mrs. Dickey, Mrs. Vanderburg and others, with an occasional visiting preacher.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: As I look back more than fifty years to those early days of teaching, I am surprised at all the things we did. We put on programs several times a year to which the whole community came. I remember especially the first year at Berry Creek we did a marionette show of "Jack and the Beanstalk." With the help of some of the mothers, especially Mrs. Vanderburg, we made and dressed the marionettes. Children of all grade levels participated, made the stage and scenery, learned to manage the strings on the puppets, made up the script and talked for the characters. A wild cucumber vine made a wonderful beanstalk, and a fresh one was always available, growing on the school ground.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: We published a school newspaper, carried on a great correspondence with one of my best friends who had moved to Baltimore, Maryland. She sent us many pictures and other things that kept a bulletin board full. In the spring we played baseball games with surrounding schools.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Of course there were a few hazards, such as a frozen water pump, getting poison oak from carrying in wood from the woodshed, oiling the schoolhouse floor, and I might add, an unexpected visit from the County School Superintendent at least once a year. The good old days when parents didn't come to school to tell you how to teach!

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: In the fall of 1940 the Berry Creek School closed because there weren't enough students. Those remaining were transported to the Tampico School, a few miles to the south. Don's brother, Ken, hauled them all in the Dickey car. I moved into Airlie to teach the upper grades (5 through 8). This was a two-story school with two high school rooms upstairs and two grade school rooms below. I taught there for two years, 1940-42, when this area became part of Camp Adair. Don and I were married in March, 1942, the second year I was at Airlie. The next year the remaining students were transported to Monmouth. Wow! The second school to close its doors after I taught there! Sounds as if my contribution to the war effort was to close the schools.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: In 1940, Clifford Stocker was the Airlie High School principal. He loved to argue, especially with the professors at Oregon State. He didn't really care which side of an argument he was on and often shifted sides in the middle. Antoinette Lambert from Salem taught the other high school room. She married Arthur Bose, who had gone to high school at Airlie with Don and Ken Dickey. The primary teacher was Mattie Swann, who had taught many years at Airlie. She had never married and had a lovely home at Lewisville. The next year, I was the only teacher who was not a Senior Citizen.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: By this time I had acquired a Model A Ford for transportation. All the teachers but Miss Swann boarded at the big McKibben house at the west edge of town. Several years ago at the annual Airlie Picnic, some of the high school boys of that time (now grandfathers) told me they used to stick a potato on the exhaust pipe of my Model A before I started home after school. I remember refereeing and keeping score for the high school girls' volley-ball games with visiting schools. I guess the most vivid memory I have of teaching at Airlie is the day the schoolhouse was on fire. When he went to stoke the furnace, the high school boy who was the janitor discovered a fire in the basement under the primary room. There being no fire department to call, after alerting the principal, he ran the two blocks to Weinert's Store for help. While we were getting the children out of the building (for a fire-drill, they thought), a bucket brigade of men appeared. They pumped water, by hand of course, from the well, passed the buckets along the line, and put out the fire. Life was often exciting, even in Airlie. The large McKibben family still consider me a member of their family.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I spent one more year teaching in the Benton County schools during the early days of World War II. This was at the Mountain View School at Lewisburg on the highway between Corvallis and Monmouth. This school is now part of the Corvallis School District. I was principal and taught grades 5 through 8. Mrs. Gertrude Gragg taught primary grades. There were four rooms in the school and a covered playshed. As I remember, we had 16 to 20 students each. At this time Don was expecting to be drafted into the Army. Camp Adair was being constructed, his family had sold their farm on Berry Creek to the government and bought another farm near Wren. Don and I were renting a tiny house, really a converted chicken- house, from John and Lucille Milbrath on Philomath Road in Corvallis. The house was cute and comfortable with a wood stove for both cooking and heating. This stove was most appreciated during the storm of 1942-43 when we had no electricity for a number of days.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Both families used it for cooking. John Milbrath was a plant pathologist at Oregon State and was largely responsible for the Rose Gardens at Avery Park. Don was working for the Oregon State Game Commission doing research on pheasant damage to farm crops. Early in 1943, I think it was February, Don was sent to Jackson County by the Fish and Wildlife Service to do Rodent Control on Camp White, which was being constructed near Medford. I stayed in Corvallis until my school term was finished in May. Don rode the bus all night Friday and back on Sunday to come home every two weeks.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: One of my worst problems during this time was my Model A and a dead battery many mornings. It was five miles to school, a bit far for hiking. Johnny Milbrath would get me started and I'd leave the car at the service station across the highway from school to have the battery recharged. Can you believe it was several weeks before they finally discovered there was a crack in the battery? Rationing was a fact of life. I got extra gas for driving to school. Meat and sugar rations were adequate. We could give coffee and cigarette coupons to friends or relatives since we did not smoke and I don't like coffee. We did not suffer. Everyone shared. There were no protest marches against the War. People did what was needed to help. Don's older brother, Leland, enlisted in the Army. Don was never taken because of his leg, and Ken was left to run the farm for his mother. My two brothers were in the Navy. People worried about their relatives in military service, wrote to them regularly, and did what was necessary at home.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Don and I were married 48-1/2 years when he died. If we had it to do over, neither of us would have changed our minds. We didn't agree on everything. We often voted differently, had different hobbies and different backgrounds, but we both operated under the same moral and ethical principles and always allowed each other to do his own thing. We also did a lot of things together. We did a good job of raising our three children. We went camping, we participated in Girl Scout and Boy Scout activities and leadership, as well as school and PTA. Don was an excellent father in every way.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: After our children were grown, I became interested in genealogy. Don took many trips with me (as long as he could keep his feet or wheels on the ground). Sometimes he urged me to go with others, especially if it required flying. He was very interested in my findings. Even where we lived was a compromise. He was raised on a farm while I was raised in Portland. We ended up on 10 acres at the edge of Eugene where he could do his farm things and I could do my city things. He was an avid hunter and fisherman. He never expected me to go hunting, but we did a lot of fishing together. We accepted each other's friends and they became mutual friends. We were two individuals who loved and respected each other. We were a good team!

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Maxine Dickey Eugene, Oregon April 8, 1991
